Predictive performance varied with buffer definition and weighting scheme. The work concerns index construction from existing geospatial records rather than sensing pedestrian environments.
label: Not related

text: Stereo vision measurement of sidewalk pinch points in dense commercial blocks. Pedestrian capacity is frequently constrained by short bottlenecks that disappear in parcel-scale width records. To address this issue, calibrated stereo cameras mounted on a walking rig reconstructed sidewalk edges and temporary objects during morning, midday and evening surveys. The effective corridor narrowed below 1.2 metres at loading zones and outdoor dining areas, with strong time-of-day variation. Repeated sensing revealed where management measures could recover usable walking space.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Perceived walkability and loneliness among older residents. A mailed questionnaire measured perceived safety, aesthetics, access to destinations and loneliness in a stratified sample of older adults. The motivation was that neighbourhood perceptions may shape social participation and wellbeing. Perceived destination access was associated with lower loneliness after demographic adjustment. All environmental information was self-reported and no physical attributes were measured with sensors.
label: Not related

text: Backpack mapping of stair-free connections in a hillside neighbourhood. A backpack system combining lidar, inertial measurement and satellite positioning captured paths, ramps, steps and handrails across the local pedestrian network. This design responds to the fact that topographic barriers make nominally nearby destinations inaccessible to people who cannot use stairs. Automatically derived elevation profiles agreed with surveyed control points and exposed several disconnected step-free route fragments. The data were used to construct mobility-specific accessibility maps.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Residential density and walking for transport in university students. Compact neighbourhoods are often assumed to encourage active travel. Accordingly, student addresses were linked to census density and destination counts, and weekly walking was reported through an online survey. Associations were modest and differed between campuses. In practical terms, the analysis uses administrative exposure indicators and self-reported behaviour.
label: Not related

text: Longitudinal change in walkability and body mass index after relocation. Moving home provides an opportunity to study environmental change. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: participants' old and new addresses were assigned values from a regional walkability database, and body mass index was measured over three follow-up waves. Relocation to higher-scoring areas was associated with a small reduction in weight gain. The environmental exposure was inherited from an existing index rather than collected through sensing.
label: Not related

text: Monocular depth estimation for curb-ramp compliance screening. Municipal curb-ramp inventories rarely contain the geometric detail required to assess usability. In the empirical work, street-level intersection images were processed with a calibrated monocular depth model to estimate ramp width, running slope, flare geometry and landing depth. A field-checked sample showed adequate accuracy for screening, while the citywide application revealed systematic deficiencies near older commercial corridors. The workflow provides a scalable basis for prioritising detailed inspection.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Meta-analysis of built environment correlates of walking. Evidence on environmental determinants of walking is distributed across disciplines. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: published effect estimates for density, connectivity, land-use mix and perceived safety were synthesised using random-effects models. Associations were strongest for transport walking and weaker for recreation. As a secondary review, the work contains no primary sensing of walkability dimensions.
label: Not related

text: Wheelchair-mounted sensing of doorway thresholds along public walking routes. A wheelchair-mounted depth camera and inertial unit recorded approach geometry at shops, civic buildings and transit facilities, with events georeferenced automatically. The motivation was that small vertical thresholds at entrances interrupt otherwise accessible pedestrian journeys. Detected threshold height and approach slope matched manual measurements, and problematic entrances clustered on streets with historic frontages. The resulting route layer captures last-metre barriers omitted from conventional sidewalk datasets.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Neighbourhood walkability and depressive symptoms during pregnancy. Daily mobility environments may affect mental health during pregnancy. To address this issue, residential walkability was assigned from census density, street connectivity and land-use data, and depressive symptoms were collected through a validated questionnaire. No consistent association remained after socioeconomic adjustment. The study tests an epidemiological relationship using pre-existing spatial data.
label: Not related

text: Mobile mapping of covered pedestrian connections between transit and hospitals. Weather-protected continuity is important for users making slow or assisted trips. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: a pedestrian-borne lidar and camera system mapped arcades, canopies, overhead links and uncovered gaps along routes from transit stops to medical facilities. Coverage length and gap duration were computed for alternative approaches, showing that nominally accessible routes differed greatly in exposure. The measurements support selection of routes that are both barrier-free and protected.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Transit-oriented development and neighbourhood walking frequency. Access to high-capacity transit may influence local walking. In the empirical work, station proximity and development intensity were derived from planning databases, while walking frequency came from repeated travel surveys. Residents near mature station areas reported more utilitarian walking. The study uses regional land-use indicators and survey outcomes without environmental sensing.
label: Not related

text: Crowdsourced smartphone video for mapping missing pedestrian links. Rapidly changing peripheral areas often lack authoritative records of where continuous walking surfaces exist. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: residents recorded geotagged smartphone video while following common routes, and frames were analysed to distinguish formal sidewalks, informal paths, road walking and discontinuities. Agreement with independent field audits was substantial and missing links were concentrated around new developments and drainage crossings. The method offers an updateable pedestrian-network evidence source.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Built environment perceptions and active ageing. Participants completed scales covering perceived traffic, aesthetics, destinations and social cohesion together with an activity questionnaire. The motivation was that supportive neighbourhoods may help older adults maintain daily activity. Perceived safety and access were associated with active ageing scores. The environmental variables are subjective responses rather than sensor-derived measurements.
label: Not related

text: Acoustic and vibration sensing of loose paving units on footways. Loose units create instability and noise but may be missed during visual inspection. A wheeled trolley equipped with microphones and accelerometers traversed stone-paved streets, and signal features were classified against annotated defect locations. The combined model distinguished loose units from ordinary joints more reliably than either sensing channel alone. Mapped defect clusters informed maintenance scheduling in the historic centre.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Walkability and diabetes medication adherence. Neighbourhood conditions may influence routines related to chronic disease management. Accordingly, patient addresses were assigned census-tract walkability scores and linked to pharmacy refill records. Higher scores showed no independent relationship with adherence after adjustment. In practical terms, the research is a health-record linkage study, not a measurement of the pedestrian environment.
label: Not related

text: Urban form and walking trip generation using travel diaries. Trip-generation models commonly include neighbourhood characteristics. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: household travel diaries were analysed alongside parcel-level density, land-use and network variables from municipal databases. Walking trips increased with destination diversity and lower car ownership. No imagery, sensors or primary environmental observations were used.
label: Not related

text: Hyperspectral classification of polished and weathered sidewalk materials. Portable hyperspectral imaging was combined with pendulum friction tests across common paving types, and spectral signatures were used to classify wear condition. This design responds to the fact that material weathering alters slip resistance while remaining difficult to judge from conventional photographs. The model separated polished from intact stone and transferred successfully to untested streets of similar material. A citywide material-risk layer was produced from targeted sensing.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Semantic sidewalk segmentation for autonomous delivery robots. A lightweight neural network segmented sidewalks, kerbs and obstacles from onboard camera images and was evaluated on robot navigation sequences. The model improved path following under shadows and partial occlusion. These observations are important because last-mile robots require real-time recognition of traversable surfaces. Its purpose is machine navigation rather than measurement of walkability dimensions for pedestrian assessment.
label: Not related

text: Haptic obstacle warning for blind travellers using depth cameras. Electronic travel aids can convey nearby hazards through vibration. A chest-mounted depth camera detected obstacles and encoded distance into a wearable haptic belt. Laboratory and corridor trials showed fewer collisions than a baseline audio cue. The system senses immediate obstacles for user guidance rather than producing walkability measurements.
label: Not related

text: Photometric stereo measurement of microtexture on pedestrian paving. Fine surface texture influences wet-weather grip but is difficult to survey continuously. In the empirical work, a compact multi-light camera captured oblique images of paving samples in situ, from which microtexture descriptors were reconstructed and calibrated against laboratory friction measurements. Low-texture zones aligned with observed slipping complaints near transit entrances. The method links image-derived surface condition to a pedestrian safety dimension.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Reinforcement learning for socially compliant robot motion. Mobile robots operating among pedestrians must avoid abrupt or intrusive trajectories. To address this issue, a policy was trained in simulated crowds and fine-tuned with recorded pedestrian trajectories. Field trials in a plaza reduced personal-space violations. The work models robot behaviour in pedestrian spaces, not the quality of those spaces.
label: Not related

text: Rain-event monitoring of ponding depth on sidewalks. Ultrasonic depth gauges and time-lapse cameras monitored known low points through multiple storms, while local topography was reconstructed from terrestrial scans. The motivation was that standing water reduces effective width and can force pedestrians into traffic. Ponding duration varied substantially even for locations with similar rainfall and was longest where blocked drainage coincided with crossfall depressions. The evidence supports drainage repairs targeted at pedestrian routes.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Tactile-paving following by an autonomous wheelchair. An onboard camera detected tactile paving and a controller adjusted steering to follow its centreline. This design responds to the fact that visual guidance can help powered wheelchairs remain on designated paths. Prototype experiments demonstrated stable tracking under moderate illumination variation. The tactile surface is used as a navigation cue rather than assessed as infrastructure.
label: Not related

text: Mapping sidewalks for robot route planning with GNSS and lidar. Autonomous platforms need globally consistent maps for long routes. The study therefore used the following approach: robot-mounted sensors generated a point-cloud map and fused GNSS constraints to reduce drift. Mapping accuracy improved in open sections and degraded beneath dense tree cover. The objective is robotic localisation and route execution.
label: Not related

text: Fall-edge detection for a smartphone travel aid. A phone-mounted lidar sensor classified ground surfaces as level, rising, descending or occluded in real time. The motivation was that people with visual impairment may benefit from warnings near stairs and platform edges. Detection accuracy was assessed during staged approaches. The device recognises hazards for immediate assistance rather than characterising walking environments at route scale.
label: Not related

text: Pedestrian trajectory forecasting for warehouse robots. Automated vehicles in manufacturing plants must anticipate worker movement. Accordingly, a diffusion-based model predicted future trajectories from past positions and map context. The model improved collision avoidance on recorded shop-floor sequences. In practical terms, the setting and objective concern industrial robot operation rather than urban walkability sensing.
label: Not related

text: Mutual-information localisation on sidewalk maps. Existing street maps could reduce the cost of robot mapping. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: laser observations from a mobile robot were aligned to two-dimensional map geometry by maximising statistical dependence. Experiments demonstrated near-real-time localisation along sidewalks. The study uses pedestrian infrastructure as a reference for robotics and does not evaluate its walkability.
label: Not related

text: Eye-tracking study of pedestrian detection of approaching bicycles. Shared crossings require pedestrians to recognise fast and quiet bicycle movements. Participants crossed instrumented paths wearing mobile eye trackers while overhead cameras recorded bicycle approach speed and yielding behaviour. Late fixation on cyclists was associated with visual clutter and oblique approach geometry. The findings identify environmental features that reduce perceptual safety for walkers.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Street-view analysis of cyclists' route preferences. Bicycle GPS trajectories were linked to segmented street-view indicators and analysed with a path-choice model. Cyclists preferred separated facilities and greener routes. These observations are important because cycling route choice may respond to greenery and roadway design. The outcome is cycling behaviour, so the work does not assess pedestrian walkability.
label: Not related

text: Night-time imaging of pedestrian conspicuity at zebra crossings. Crossing markings and lighting jointly determine whether waiting pedestrians are visible to drivers. To address this issue, calibrated low-light cameras recorded staged pedestrian presence under existing luminaires, and contrast ratios were computed for clothing, background and approach direction. Several crossings meeting average illuminance guidance still produced poor pedestrian-background contrast. The assessment adds visibility evidence to conventional lighting inventories.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Roadside camera monitoring of e-scooter helmet compliance. Rapid micromobility growth has created enforcement challenges. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: traffic cameras and object detection were used to classify helmet use, riding location and speed. Compliance varied by infrastructure type and ownership model. The sensing concerns rider behaviour and road-rule compliance rather than pedestrian-environment measurement.
label: Not related

text: Pressure-mat sensing of waiting-space crowding at transit crossings. Thin pressure mats and overhead depth cameras measured occupancy and standing distribution at crossings beside busy transit stops. This design responds to the fact that crowded waiting areas can spill pedestrians into the carriageway before the signal changes. Spillover occurred when shelter placement reduced usable waiting depth, particularly during vehicle arrival peaks. The results quantify a design interaction between transit facilities and pedestrian crossing comfort.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Vehicle-mounted vibration detection of carriageway potholes. Fleet-based sensing can accelerate road maintenance. Accelerometers on buses recorded vertical shocks that were classified and georeferenced. Detected potholes were confirmed through road inspection. The pilot covered arterial and residential road segments under different traffic loads.. The target is the vehicle carriageway, not surfaces used by pedestrians.
label: Not related

text: Computer vision measurement of parking-search behaviour. Searching for curb parking may affect driving performance. To address this issue, instrumented vehicles recorded gaze, speed and lane position while drivers searched for spaces. Search periods produced longer off-road glances and slower travel. The study measures driver behaviour rather than walkability.
label: Not related

text: Mobile lidar analysis of sight obstruction at driveway crossings. Vehicle exits across sidewalks create conflict where walls and planting restrict mutual visibility. The study therefore used the following approach: a backpack lidar survey reconstructed sight triangles from pedestrian eye height at commercial and residential driveways. Available sight distance was compared with observed vehicle emergence speeds and verified through field photography. Locations with severe obstruction were mapped for vegetation trimming and setback intervention.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Cyclist conflict detection at signalised intersections. Automated trajectory analysis can reveal near misses not captured in crash records. The study therefore used the following approach: video tracking reconstructed cyclist and vehicle paths and computed surrogate safety indicators. Conflicts concentrated during permitted turning phases. The analysis concerns bicycle safety and intersection operation rather than walkability sensing.
label: Not related

text: Audio detection of accessible pedestrian signal operation. Binaural recorders positioned at waiting points captured signal tones and background noise across different traffic periods. The motivation was that audible crossing cues may be installed but inaudible under real traffic conditions. Signal-to-noise ratios fell below recognisable levels at several intersections despite functioning equipment. The method assesses the effective, rather than nominal, availability of an accessibility aid.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: E-scooter surface-vibration mapping on cycle tracks. Surface quality affects micromobility comfort and vehicle stability. In the empirical work, accelerometers mounted on shared scooters recorded vibration along designated cycling facilities. Roughness hotspots corresponded with pavement joints and utility covers. The sensing is specific to scooter travel and not pedestrian walking conditions.
label: Not related

text: Distributed black-globe sensing of radiant heat along treeless corridors. Air temperature alone understates thermal burden on exposed walking routes. Accordingly, compact black-globe and humidity sensors were mounted at pedestrian height along parallel shaded and unshaded streets for an entire warm season. Radiant-temperature differences persisted into the evening and explained route-level comfort ratings better than the nearest weather station. In practical terms, the network identifies where shade interventions would most improve walking conditions.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Automatic lane-marking inventory from road survey imagery. Vehicle-mounted cameras and deep learning detected centre lines, edge lines and turn arrows. The motivation was that accurate markings support road safety and maintenance planning. The inventory achieved high agreement with highway records. Although sidewalks appear in some images, the target is roadway infrastructure.
label: Not related

text: Mobile ozone exposure mapping on school walking trips. Children may encounter sharp pollutant gradients that fixed monitors cannot resolve. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: calibrated ozone sensors and GNSS loggers were carried along repeated school routes at morning and afternoon periods. Exposure peaks occurred near sunlit intersections with queuing traffic and differed from particulate-matter patterns measured simultaneously. The study demonstrates route-specific environmental sensing relevant to healthy walking.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Radar-based estimation of vehicle yielding at roundabouts. Driver yielding influences traffic operation and crash risk. Accordingly, roadside radar and video measured approach speed, gap acceptance and queue formation. Yielding rates varied with entry geometry and traffic volume. In practical terms, pedestrian-environment attributes were not measured.
label: Not related

text: Shared-bicycle demand forecasting with smartcard and weather data. Operators require reliable forecasts for rebalancing. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: trip records, station capacity and meteorological variables were used in a spatiotemporal model. Forecast accuracy improved during commuting peaks. The work predicts bicycle demand rather than sensing walkability dimensions.
label: Not related

text: Wearable obstacle warning for visually impaired indoor navigation. The system was tested in office corridors with blindfolded participants. Outcomes included collision count and task time. A chest-mounted camera detected doors, furniture and people and translated them into haptic cues. Haptic guidance reduced collisions in office corridors, although users required practice to interpret dense obstacle scenes.
label: Not related

text: Deep learning prediction of residential prices from street imagery. Street-view features were extracted with a convolutional network and added to hedonic price models. Facade condition and greenery improved prediction accuracy. These observations are important because visual characteristics may explain housing-market variation. The purpose is property valuation, not assessment of the pedestrian environment.
label: Not related

text: Continuous carbon monoxide sensing in covered pedestrian passages. Semi-enclosed walkways near traffic may accumulate pollutants even when outdoor monitors report acceptable conditions. Low-cost carbon monoxide and ventilation sensors were installed in arcades, underpasses and open comparison segments. Short-duration peaks coincided with delivery activity and weak airflow in passages with limited openings. The observations support ventilation and access-management interventions.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Panoramic detection of alcohol advertising exposure. Public-health surveillance may benefit from remote observation of marketing. Street panoramas were coded automatically for branded signs and retail displays. Detection rates were compared with field observation. The measured outcome is commercial advertising, not a dimension of pedestrian walkability.
label: Not related

text: Street-view estimation of neighbourhood carbon emissions. Urban visual form may act as a proxy for energy and transport intensity. To address this issue, segmented imagery and demographic data were used in gradient-boosting models. Vehicle presence and building density were the strongest predictors. The study targets emissions estimation rather than walking conditions.
label: Not related

text: Personal noise dosimetry during barrier-free route alternatives. Wheelchair users and pedestrians carried dosimeters and location loggers along step-free alternatives between transit and public services. This design responds to the fact that the most accessible path is not necessarily the most comfortable acoustic environment. Routes requiring detours beside arterial roads produced markedly higher cumulative exposure than shorter stepped routes. The findings reveal an environmental trade-off within accessible route planning.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Image-based mapping of architectural heritage styles. Facade photographs were processed to identify period, ornament and material. This design responds to the fact that automated classification can support conservation inventories. The resulting map distinguished historic districts. Pedestrian-scale imagery is present, but the objective is heritage documentation.
label: Not related

text: Acoustic sensing of urban bird diversity. Autonomous recorders provide scalable biodiversity monitoring. The study therefore used the following approach: audio nodes in parks captured seasonal bird calls that were classified by species. Richness increased with vegetation complexity. The acoustic measurements concern ecology, not sound conditions experienced by pedestrians.
label: Not related

text: Particle-number concentration along signalised pedestrian crossings. Short waits beside accelerating traffic may contribute disproportionately to inhaled exposure. In the empirical work, fast-response particle counters were carried by pedestrians during repeated crossings and waiting periods at intersections with different signal phasing. Concentrations spiked during the first acceleration wave and were reduced where waiting areas were set back behind planting buffers. The study quantifies a highly localised dimension of route healthfulness.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Street imagery and machine learning for crime prediction. Segmented street-view indicators were combined with police records in predictive models. The motivation was that visual disorder and land use may correlate with local crime. Model interpretation identified nonlinear associations. The study uses streetscape data to explain crime rather than measuring pedestrian walking quality.
label: Not related

text: Radiant asymmetry measurement beneath reflective building facades. Six-directional radiometers and thermal cameras measured pedestrian-level radiation beside reflective and non-reflective facades through clear days. The motivation was that highly reflective glazing can redirect solar radiation onto sidewalks. Localized exposure peaks shifted with solar angle and exceeded those predicted from shade maps alone. The results identify design conditions that undermine nominally shaded walking space.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Mobile mapping of bridge clearance for freight routing. Oversize vehicles require reliable vertical-clearance information. Accordingly, vehicle-mounted lidar measured clearance beneath bridges and overhead structures. The inventory reduced routing errors for freight operators. In practical terms, the sensing is directed at vehicle movement, not pedestrian accessibility.
label: Not related

text: Thermal imaging of building-envelope heat loss. District retrofit programmes require rapid screening of inefficient buildings. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: vehicle-mounted thermal cameras surveyed facades during winter nights. Anomalies were associated with poorly insulated components. The measurements concern building performance rather than pedestrian thermal comfort.
label: Not related

text: Vision-based illegal-dumping detection for cleansing operations. Service-vehicle imagery was analysed to detect bags, bulky waste and overflowing containers. Alerts shortened removal times in pilot districts. These observations are important because rapid identification of waste accumulation can improve municipal response. The system manages street cleansing and does not assess walking conditions.
label: Not related

text: Multi-season pollen exposure monitoring on recreational walking loops. Vegetated routes may provide shade while increasing allergen exposure for sensitive pedestrians. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: wearable pollen samplers and GNSS tracking were used on loops through parks, tree-lined streets and built-up corridors across flowering seasons. Peak exposure depended on species composition and wind direction rather than green-view index alone. The measurements reveal a seasonal trade-off in the healthfulness of walking environments.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Street-view classification of retail business types. Fine-grained land-use data are often outdated. Storefront images and text recognition were used to assign commercial categories. The resulting database improved retail-mix estimates. Predictions were aggregated by block to update a municipal commercial database.. The work inventories economic activity and does not measure walkability directly.
label: Not related

text: Night-time luminance imaging of facial recognition distance. Pedestrians may feel unsafe where faces cannot be recognised at ordinary interpersonal distance. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: calibrated cameras recorded human targets along residential paths under existing lighting, and recognition contrast was modelled at increasing distances. Recognition distance varied more with light distribution and background brightness than with mean illuminance. The metric provides a human-centred assessment of night walking environments.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Camera-based monitoring of construction progress. Frequent visual records can support project control. To address this issue, fixed cameras and object detection tracked completion of structural elements against schedules. The system identified delays earlier than manual reporting. The sensing occurs on building sites and is unrelated to pedestrian-environment assessment.
label: Not related

text: Seasonal green-view sensing from pedestrian-mounted panoramic cameras. Single-date imagery can misrepresent the visual greenery available across the year. Panoramic cameras collected repeated routes during leaf-on, leaf-off and flowering periods, and semantic segmentation quantified visible vegetation by height band. Seasonal variation was greatest on streets dominated by deciduous canopy and climbing vegetation. The dataset enables time-sensitive evaluation of visual walkability.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Computational fluid dynamics optimisation of street-canyon trees. Vegetation can alter both heat and pollutant dispersion. The study therefore used the following approach: a series of CFD simulations varied canopy size, building ratio and wind direction. Pareto-optimal configurations balanced thermal and air-quality objectives. No pedestrian-level field sensing was undertaken.
label: Not related

text: Agent-based simulation of shade-seeking pedestrian routes. Pedestrians may accept longer paths to remain in shade. In the empirical work, agents navigated a digital street network using modelled solar shadows and synthetic demand. Scenarios predicted route shifts after tree planting. The study simulates behaviour without observing or sensing actual walking environments.
label: Not related

text: Image segmentation of construction hoarding quality on pedestrian routes. Repeated street imagery was segmented to measure hoarding continuity, lighting, viewing panels, graffiti and residual walkway width. This design responds to the fact that temporary works can reduce both visual quality and perceived security for months. Long-duration sites with opaque, poorly maintained hoardings received the lowest pedestrian ratings. The monitoring framework captures a temporary but consequential walkability condition.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Depth-enhanced measurement of ground-floor setback and edge definition. The relationship between facades and the walking corridor affects enclosure and activity. The study therefore used the following approach: street imagery with monocular depth estimation reconstructed setback, forecourt depth and continuity of the building line. Derived indicators distinguished streets with similar building density but very different pedestrian-scale spatial definition. The method adds three-dimensional detail to visual walkability assessment.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: ENVI-met modelling of thermal comfort on a proposed boulevard. Design alternatives can be compared before construction. Accordingly, microclimate simulations tested tree spacing, paving and building setbacks. Predicted comfort improved under continuous canopy. Alternative designs were assessed under representative summer weather scenarios.. In practical terms, no on-site environmental observations were collected.
label: Not related

text: Automated mapping of pedestrian-scale landmark visibility. Visible landmarks support orientation and reduce uncertainty on complex walking routes. In the empirical work, panoramic images were processed to detect selected civic landmarks and estimate the route length from which each remained visible. Visibility gaps corresponded with locations where unfamiliar pedestrians made navigation errors in a separate tracking exercise. The metric links visual sensing to wayfinding quality.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Microscopic pedestrian simulation of station evacuation. Emergency design requires testing high-demand scenarios. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: a calibrated simulation model reproduced queues and exit use under alternative incidents. Layout changes reduced predicted clearance time. The analysis is computational and does not sense existing pedestrian conditions.
label: Not related

text: Solar-geometry model of sidewalk shade provision. Three-dimensional city models and sun-position calculations generated hourly shade maps. Projected coverage varied by street orientation. These observations are important because building form determines the timing of shade. The method estimates conditions from geometry without ground-level sensing or validation.
label: Not related

text: Repeated imagery assessment of storefront vacancy and visual change. Rapid frontage turnover can alter the perceived vitality of walking streets. Accordingly, georegistered images from quarterly surveys were analysed for shutters, empty displays, temporary signage and occupied entrances. The resulting change index detected decline earlier than annual business registers and aligned with reductions in pedestrian dwell. In practical terms, the method supports longitudinal sensing of streetscape vitality.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Traffic-noise propagation modelling along walking corridors. Noise maps can support planning where measurements are sparse. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: road traffic inputs and building geometry were used in a standard acoustic model. Predicted levels identified exposed corridors. The study models noise rather than collecting pedestrian-level acoustic data.
label: Not related

text: Rendered streetscape preference experiment. Design elements can be varied systematically in computer-generated scenes. Participants rated virtual streets with different greenery, widths and facades. Preferences increased with tree cover and active frontage. The controlled presentation isolated the effect of each design variable.. The images are survey stimuli, not sensor observations of real environments.
label: Not related

text: Polarised imaging of glare on glazed pedestrian corridors. Specular reflections can impair visual comfort and obstacle detection. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: polarised cameras recorded glare intensity along routes bordered by glass facades and polished paving under different sun angles. High-glare segments were associated with reduced fixation on low-contrast pavement hazards in a companion eye-tracking study. The measurements identify a visual comfort dimension absent from standard audits.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Digital-twin simulation of crowd movement in a public square. Scenario testing can reveal potential congestion before events. To address this issue, synthetic agents moved through a detailed three-dimensional model under alternative demand assumptions. The simulation identified bottleneck entrances. Demand levels and entrance closures were varied systematically across scenarios.. No empirical pedestrian sensing was performed.
label: Not related

text: Electrodermal sensing of stress at sidewalk-cyclist conflict points. Pedestrians wore electrodermal and heart-rate sensors on repeated routes while video documented passing distance and bicycle speed. Arousal peaks were concentrated at narrow sections with overtaking from behind and were reproducible across participants. These observations are important because shared or poorly separated facilities may generate stress even when crashes are rare. The study localises a human-response dimension of perceived walkability.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Validation of step counters in cane users. Activity monitors may miscount steps when mobility aids are used. In the empirical work, leg- and cane-mounted devices were compared with video counts across indoor surfaces. Leg placement provided higher accuracy. The study evaluates a clinical measurement device, not walkability.
label: Not related

text: Accelerometer assessment of physical activity in adolescents. Students wore wrist accelerometers for seven days and completed health questionnaires. The motivation was that objective activity measurement can reduce recall bias. Activity declined with age and differed by sex. Valid wear time and intensity thresholds followed a standard population-health protocol.. No pedestrian environmental dimension was sensed.
label: Not related

text: Inertial sensing of gait adaptation to uneven urban surfaces. People alter step timing and balance strategy when pavement becomes difficult. To address this issue, older and younger adults traversed real footway segments wearing shoe and trunk inertial sensors, with surface geometry captured independently by lidar. Step variability increased sharply beyond a roughness threshold and was more pronounced among older participants. The study relates measured environment condition to embodied walking difficulty.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Skin-temperature response to shade transitions during summer walking. Participants wore skin-temperature and heart-rate sensors while walking routes with distinct shade patterns, and microclimate was logged continuously. This design responds to the fact that rapid alternation between sun and shade may influence comfort differently from average exposure. Long continuous shade produced faster physiological recovery than fragmented shade of equivalent total duration. The results inform how shade continuity should be represented in walkability metrics.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Pressure-insole analysis of running on different surfaces. Foot loading varies with surface stiffness and speed. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: runners completed controlled trials while pressure and motion sensors recorded biomechanics. Peak forces differed between track and concrete. The study examines running mechanics, not pedestrian-environment walkability.
label: Not related

text: Wearable adherence in a school physical-activity programme. Students received activity bands and adherence was analysed against survey characteristics. Perceived neighbourhood safety predicted continued device use. These observations are important because long-term use determines the value of consumer trackers. The environmental measure was self-reported and the sensor captured personal activity only.
label: Not related

text: Gaze and postural response to cluttered sidewalk obstacles. Avoiding multiple obstacles requires visual attention and lateral manoeuvring. In the empirical work, participants walked commercial streets wearing eye trackers and inertial units while mapped objects supplied obstruction type and position. Dense low-level clutter increased downward gaze, trunk rotation and route deviation. The combined signals provide an objective measure of navigational burden.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Cardiorespiratory response to treadmill walking. Exercise testing can quantify functional capacity. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: participants walked at graded speeds while oxygen uptake and heart rate were recorded. Responses distinguished clinical fitness groups. The controlled laboratory protocol does not assess urban walking environments.
label: Not related

text: Ambulatory stress sensing around vacant and poorly maintained frontages. Participants completed matched urban routes wearing electrodermal sensors and provided brief geolocated ratings, while imagery quantified frontage condition. The motivation was that visual disorder may affect comfort differently during actual walking than in image-rating experiments. Elevated arousal was consistently associated with long vacant edges and concealed entrances after controlling for traffic noise. The study links sensed human response to observable streetscape conditions.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: IMU classification of rehabilitation exercises. Automatic recognition can support remote therapy. Multiple inertial units classified prescribed lower-limb activities. The model achieved high accuracy across patients. Signals were collected during supervised sessions and evaluated with participant-independent validation.. The sensing target is exercise performance rather than walkability.
label: Not related

text: Wi-Fi and thermal counting of pedestrian dwell in civic squares. Simple entry counts do not distinguish passage from meaningful use of public space. Accordingly, anonymous wireless detections were fused with thermal-camera tracks to estimate visit duration and movement zones without retaining identifiable imagery. Dwell increased near shaded seating and declined sharply during high radiant heat. In practical terms, the approach measures how environmental quality influences pedestrian use.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Wearable monitoring of construction-worker workload. Workers wore heart-rate and motion sensors throughout shifts. This design responds to the fact that physical strain varies across occupational tasks. High-strain periods clustered during material handling. Task categories were annotated by observers for comparison with the sensor-derived estimates.. The occupational environment and outcome are unrelated to walkability assessment.
label: Not related

text: Airborne lidar estimation of municipal tree-canopy cover. Consistent canopy metrics support urban forestry targets. The study therefore used the following approach: airborne point clouds were classified to delineate vegetation and summarised by district. Canopy inequality persisted across acquisition years. The analysis relies on overhead sensing and does not represent pedestrian-level experience.
label: Not related

text: Satellite NDVI and neighbourhood health outcomes. Greenness exposure may influence population health. In the empirical work, multispectral imagery produced vegetation indices around residential addresses and was linked to health surveys. Higher greenness was associated with better wellbeing. The study does not sense walking routes or pedestrian-scale environmental conditions.
label: Not related

text: Depth-camera analysis of passing behaviour around mobility-aid users. Sidewalk width standards should reflect interactions involving slower and wider users. Overhead depth cameras recorded encounters between general pedestrians and people using wheelchairs, walkers or pushchairs on different path widths. Narrow sections produced longer following and more aborted passing attempts. The evidence supports inclusive capacity assessment of pedestrian routes.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Aerial extraction of road and sidewalk classes for mapping. Overhead imagery can improve base-map completeness. Accordingly, a segmentation model delineated roads, sidewalks and buildings from orthophotos. Accuracy varied under tree canopy. Outputs were evaluated as map features rather than as pedestrian-scale conditions.. In practical terms, the purpose is top-down cartographic mapping without pedestrian-perspective assessment.
label: Not related

text: Satellite classification of urban impervious surfaces. Impervious-cover data support stormwater planning. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: multispectral scenes were classified with convolutional and transformer models. The resulting map improved estimates of runoff potential. Training samples represented built-up, vegetation, water and bare-soil classes.. No pedestrian environmental dimension was measured.
label: Not related

text: Bluetooth sensing of route redistribution after a new crossing. Infrastructure changes may alter pedestrian route choice beyond the immediate site. To address this issue, calibrated Bluetooth detectors were placed on parallel streets before and after a signalised crossing opened, with manual counts used to estimate device detection rates. The treated route gained users while an informal crossing path declined. The network captures behavioural response to pedestrian infrastructure.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Airborne thermal mapping of urban heat islands. Thermal imagery from aircraft was related to land cover and building density. Hotspots concentrated in industrial districts. These observations are important because citywide surface temperature patterns inform climate adaptation. The measurement is roof- and surface-oriented rather than pedestrian-level thermal exposure.
label: Not related

text: Trajectory sensing of informal desire lines across public housing estates. Privacy-preserving overhead sensors recorded movement through open spaces across seasons, and recurrent trajectories were compared with paved connections. This design responds to the fact that official paths may not reflect the routes pedestrians actually use. Persistent desire lines formed where formal routes added distance or avoided shaded edges. The results identify network changes likely to improve everyday walkability.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: National lidar inventory of streetscape objects from above. Dense point clouds enable volumetric urban analysis. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: airborne lidar was voxelised to estimate trees, walls and overhead structures. Small-object detection improved with higher pulse density. The aerial acquisition does not measure conditions from the walking perspective.
label: Not related

text: Automated measurement of pedestrian hesitation at complex junctions. Pause and reversal behaviour can indicate uncertainty even when trips are completed. The study therefore used the following approach: video tracking reconstructed trajectories at multi-leg intersections, and hesitation events were detected from speed and heading changes. Events clustered at locations with discontinuous markings and ambiguous refuge alignment. The indicator provides behavioural evidence of route legibility.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: RFID-assisted audit of accessible public toilets along walking routes. Availability of usable toilets influences how far some people can walk independently. In the empirical work, facilities were equipped with anonymous availability beacons and surveyed for entrance width, step-free access and opening status over six months. Nominal provision overstated practical availability because closures and inaccessible entrances were common. The combined data improve amenity-based assessment of pedestrian accessibility.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Systematic review of sensor technologies for pedestrian studies. Rapid technological development has produced diverse measurement approaches. To address this issue, published studies using imagery, lidar, wearables and environmental sensors were screened and synthesised. Evidence gaps were identified for low-income settings and accessibility outcomes. As a review, the article introduces no primary sensing data.
label: Not related

text: Text mining of municipal plans for walking commitments. Natural-language processing classified references to sidewalks, crossings and pedestrian safety across planning documents. This design responds to the fact that policy documents reveal how active travel priorities are framed. Specific commitments remained less common than general support. The data source is text, not the physical walking environment.
label: Not related

text: Machine-vision inventory of drinking fountains and bottle-filling points. Street and park imagery was processed to detect fountains, operating controls and surrounding clearance, with field checks confirming functionality. The motivation was that water access can support walking in hot climates but is rarely represented in route information. Large gaps existed between working facilities along popular recreational routes. The inventory adds a climate-relevant pedestrian amenity.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Ultrasonic sensing of temporary scaffolding clearance. Construction scaffolds can leave widths that vary along a single installation. Accordingly, compact ultrasonic units mounted on inspection trolleys measured lateral and overhead clearance beneath scaffolding across active works sites. Critical pinch points were associated with diagonal braces and stored materials rather than nominal scaffold width. In practical terms, the method supports objective compliance monitoring of temporary walking corridors.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Delphi study on indicators for inclusive walkability. Expert consensus can guide indicator selection. In the empirical work, a panel rated the relevance and feasibility of candidate accessibility, safety and comfort measures over three rounds. Consensus was reached on a core indicator set. The research develops a framework but does not collect sensor observations.
label: Not related

text: Street-image recognition of pedestrian information maps and route markers. Orientation aids are useful only when visible, legible and positioned at decision points. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: images captured from pedestrian approach directions were analysed to detect maps, directional signs and marker continuity. Several routes had high sign counts but poor decision-point coverage. The resulting continuity metric reflects functional wayfinding support.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Policy evaluation of a complete-streets ordinance. Capital-project documents and council records were analysed before and after ordinance adoption. The motivation was that legislation may change investment priorities. Pedestrian provisions became more frequent in funded projects. The study evaluates policy implementation rather than sensing street conditions.
label: Not related

text: Mobile mapping of litter-bin obstruction around bus stops. Range data and imagery were used to map bins, poles, shelters and waiting passengers around bus stops at peak periods. Object configurations reduced clear paths below accessible thresholds at a substantial share of stops. These observations are important because amenity placement can unintentionally reduce boarding and through-walking space. The analysis supports coordinated placement of street furniture.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Qualitative study of barriers to walking in informal settlements. Residents possess detailed knowledge of everyday mobility constraints. Accordingly, focus groups and walking interviews explored safety, drainage and social barriers. Participants emphasised harassment and seasonal flooding. In practical terms, the evidence is qualitative and no sensor-based measurement was undertaken.
label: Not related

text: Time-of-flight monitoring of outdoor dining expansion. Seasonal terraces alter footway capacity and pedestrian movement. The proposed workflow combined field acquisition and analysis: time-of-flight sensors measured the occupied envelope of tables and chairs at regular intervals, while cameras recorded pedestrian diversion behaviour. Encroachment exceeded permitted boundaries most often during evening peaks and at corners. The study provides continuous evidence for managing shared sidewalk space.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Bibliometric mapping of walkability research themes. The field spans public health, transport and urban design. Data collection and analysis were organised as follows: publication metadata, keywords and citation networks were analysed to identify thematic clusters. Technology-based assessment emerged as a growing topic. The study maps literature rather than sensing pedestrian environments.
label: Not related

text: Estimating effective sidewalk width under obstruction using fused imagery and range data. Nominal sidewalk width overstates the space actually available to pedestrians because poles, signage, parked vehicles and street furniture reduce the usable corridor. We fused street-level panoramic images with synchronised lidar returns to segment the paved surface and to detect intruding objects. Effective width was then computed as the largest obstruction-free corridor at each location. Across a downtown study area, effective width was on average 0.9 m narrower than the cadastral value, and 18 percent of segments fell below the minimum required for two-way pedestrian flow.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Pedestrian gaze behaviour in commercial streets recorded with mobile eye tracking. Understanding which streetscape elements attract visual attention supports design of more engaging pedestrian environments. Participants walked instrumented routes wearing mobile eye-tracking glasses while their gaze was mapped onto segmented panoramic imagery of the same corridors. Fixation duration was aggregated by streetscape element class. Vegetation, shopfront displays and other pedestrians accounted for the majority of fixations, while blank walls and parked vehicles received disproportionately little attention despite occupying large visual angles.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Neighbourhood walkability and accelerometer-measured physical activity in a cohort of middle-aged adults. Physical inactivity remains a major risk factor for chronic disease. This cohort study examined whether residential neighbourhood walkability is associated with objectively measured physical activity. Participants wore hip-mounted accelerometers for seven consecutive days, and moderate-to-vigorous activity was derived using established cut-points. Walkability was assigned from a published composite index combining residential density, intersection density and land use mix at the census tract level. After adjustment for age, sex, income and education, participants in the highest walkability quartile accumulated significantly more daily activity minutes.
label: Not related

text: Built environment exposure and body mass index trajectories in children. Childhood obesity is influenced by the environments in which children live. Using longitudinal data from a national cohort, this study examined associations between changes in neighbourhood built environment characteristics and trajectories of body mass index and waist circumference. Environmental exposures were derived from administrative land use and road network databases linked to residential addresses. Anthropometric outcomes were measured biennially by trained assessors. Growth curve models indicated that children experiencing increases in destination accessibility showed slower increases in body mass index.
label: Not related

text: Objectively measured sleep and residential walkability among adult women. Sleep is influenced by environmental context. Participants in a prospective cohort wore wrist actigraphy devices for one week and carried GPS loggers to characterise mobility beyond the residential address. Walkability was obtained from an existing national index and assigned both to home location and to GPS-derived activity space. Associations between walkability and sleep duration and efficiency were examined with mixed models. Activity-space walkability showed weak associations with sleep efficiency, while residential walkability showed none after adjustment.
label: Not related

text: Development of a network-based walkability scoring system for a metropolitan region. Existing area-based walkability measures provide coarse spatial resolution and treat all residents identically. This paper proposes a scoring system in which nodes of the road network, rather than administrative units, serve as the unit of analysis. Scores combine intersection density, destination counts within network buffers, and slope derived from a digital elevation model. The approach is demonstrated for a metropolitan region and compared against a conventional area-based index. Results show substantially finer spatial differentiation, particularly at neighbourhood edges.
label: Not related

text: Walkability of historic city centres under climate change scenarios. This study defines a methodology to compute a walkability index for tourist cities and to project its evolution under climate scenarios. The index combines street network connectivity, slope, land use diversity and shading potential derived from building footprints and cadastral records. Projected temperature and humidity from regional climate models were used to adjust a comfort component of the index for mid-century and end-of-century horizons. Application to three heritage cities shows a pronounced decline of summer walkability, concentrated in unshaded open squares.
label: Not related

text: Comparing walkability indices across three metropolitan regions using open geospatial data. Numerous walkability indices exist but are rarely compared on a common basis. This paper computes four widely used composite indices for three metropolitan regions using harmonised open geospatial datasets, including road centrelines, building footprints, land use parcels and transit stop locations. Agreement between indices is assessed with rank correlations and spatial cluster analysis. Substantial divergence was observed at fine spatial scales, indicating that the choice of index materially affects which neighbourhoods are classified as walkable.
label: Not related

text: Street-level environment and cyclists' route choice modelled from GPS trajectories and imagery. Understanding cyclist route preferences supports infrastructure planning. GPS trajectories from a bicycle-sharing system were map-matched to the cycling network, and street view imagery along candidate routes was segmented to quantify greenery, road surface and building presence. A path size logit model estimated the influence of these attributes on route choice. Cyclists showed a consistent preference for segments with higher vegetation and separated facilities, and were willing to accept longer distances to obtain them.
label: Not related

text: Bikeability assessment framework for an island city using multi-source data. Cycling-friendly environments are essential for sustainable mobility. This study develops a multi-scale bikeability framework combining network connectivity, gradient, facility separation and street-level visual attributes extracted from imagery. Indicators were weighted through expert elicitation and aggregated at three spatial scales. Application to an island city identified corridors where infrastructure provision diverges from latent demand estimated from shared bicycle trip records.
label: Not related

text: Micromobility rider compliance monitored with roadside cameras and machine learning. Growth in shared and private e-scooter use has raised concerns about rider behaviour. Traffic cameras at eight urban sites captured more than 600,000 observations of riders over two years, processed with a detection and classification pipeline. Helmet use, riding speed and footway incursion were coded automatically and verified on a manual subsample. Compliance with helmet requirements was low and declined over the study period, while speeds exceeded posted limits at a majority of observed sites.
label: Not related

text: Real-time sidewalk and road segmentation for autonomous mobile robot navigation. Sidewalk delivery robots must distinguish traversable from non-traversable surfaces in real time. This paper presents a parallelised lidar processing pipeline integrated within a robot operating framework, achieving processing rates above 20 Hz on embedded hardware. Ground plane extraction, kerb detection and surface classification are performed sequentially. Evaluation on public benchmarks and on data collected by the robot platform demonstrates improved precision over prior approaches while reducing computational load.
label: Not related

text: Visual servoing control for an autonomous wheelchair following tactile paving. This study addresses the urban mobility problem of people with walking disabilities by proposing a control system for an autonomous wheelchair. A linearised wheelchair model is developed and image-based visual servoing is introduced to track yellow tactile paving. Reference paths are generated using robust vanishing point estimation and Hough line detection. Simulation and prototype experiments demonstrate stable tracking performance under varying illumination and partial occlusion of the tactile surface.
label: Not related

text: Airborne lidar voxel analysis of streetscape features at national scale. This study investigates extraction of streetscape features from high-density airborne lidar collected under a national mapping programme. Point clouds were classified and aggregated into three-dimensional voxel zones bounded by proximal polygons. Buildings, street trees, walls, poles and overhead lines were quantified volumetrically. The work demonstrates that denser acquisition standards permit detection of smaller features than previously possible, and proposes descriptive statistics for characterising streetscapes in three dimensions from aerial acquisition alone.
label: Not related

text: Satellite-derived greenness and residential neighbourhood characteristics. This analysis characterises neighbourhood vegetation using multispectral satellite imagery and vegetation indices computed at multiple buffer radii around residential addresses. Temporal composites were generated to reduce cloud and seasonal effects. Associations between derived greenness and area-level socioeconomic indicators were examined. Results show persistent inequalities in vegetation exposure, with the magnitude of the association depending strongly on the buffer radius selected.
label: Not related

text: Pedestrian crash exposure modelling with geographically weighted regression. Reliable exposure measures are needed for pedestrian safety analysis. This study develops surrogate exposure models for urban road networks using sociodemographic attributes, land use categories and network geometric characteristics obtained from municipal databases. Several geographically weighted regression specifications were compared using goodness-of-fit and residual spatial autocorrelation criteria. The semiparametric specification performed best, and the resulting exposure estimates were used to normalise observed pedestrian crash frequencies across zones.
label: Not related

text: Spatiotemporal parameters during overground walking in adults with lower limb impairment. Understanding walking mechanics informs clinical intervention. Participants completed overground walking trials at self-selected speed while instrumented with inertial measurement units at the pelvis and lower limbs. Step time, step length asymmetry and double support duration were extracted and compared between impaired and control groups. Significant asymmetries were observed and were associated with self-reported mobility limitation scores.
label: Not related

text: Predicting residential property values from street-level imagery with deep learning. Housing markets respond to visual characteristics of the surrounding environment that are difficult to quantify in conventional hedonic models. This study extracts visual features from street-level imagery using a convolutional network and incorporates them into price prediction models alongside structural and locational attributes. Models including visual features achieved a marked reduction in prediction error. Interpretation analysis indicates that facade condition and streetscape greenery contribute most to the improvement.
label: Not related

text: Estimating neighbourhood carbon emissions from street view imagery. This work explores whether visual characteristics of urban streets carry information about neighbourhood-level carbon emissions. Street view images were processed with a segmentation network and derived visual indicators were combined with building and demographic attributes in gradient boosting models. Emissions inventories at neighbourhood level served as the target variable. Predictive performance was moderate, and interpretation indicated that building density and vehicle presence dominated the visual signal.
label: Not related

text: Detecting outdoor alcohol marketing in urban environments using panoramic imagery. Controls on alcohol marketing are a public health intervention of growing interest. This study compared the efficiency of remote coding of panoramic street imagery against on-street observation by trained teams for recording alcohol sale points, advertising and promotional materials along sampled street stretches. Agreement between methods was assessed for each data category. Remote coding achieved comparable results for permanent signage but underperformed for temporary displays.
label: Not related

text: Agent-based simulation of shade-seeking pedestrian movement. Pedestrians adapt their routes to avoid solar exposure, which conventional shortest-path models ignore. This paper presents an agent-based model in which agents weight route segments by simulated shadow availability derived from building geometry and solar position. Scenario experiments explore how added tree planting alters aggregate route distributions. Model outputs are compared with synthetic demand profiles; empirical validation with observed pedestrian trajectories is identified as future work.
label: Not related

text: Stated preference assessment of pedestrian comfort in a South Asian city. Understanding how pedestrians perceive their environment is essential for prioritising interventions. A stated preference experiment presented respondents with tailored street-level scenes varying in sidewalk provision, traffic conditions and encroachment. More than two thousand participants rated perceived exposure and comfort, and sociodemographic and travel behaviour data were collected. Multivariate models related scene attributes to perception outcomes. Absence of sidewalks and encroachment by two-wheelers were the strongest negative contributors.
label: Not related

text: Perceptions of walkable space and geographic identity among urban residents. Walkability has expanded across disciplines and now operates at multiple scales with heterogeneous definitions, raising concerns about conceptual coherence. This paper examines how residents' identification with their locality shapes their evaluation of walkable space. Semi-structured interviews and a structured questionnaire were administered in three neighbourhoods. Findings indicate that place attachment moderates the relationship between reported environmental attributes and overall walkability evaluation, suggesting limits to purely physical accounts of the concept.
label: Not related

text: Continuous kerb height profiling along pedestrian routes using vehicle-mounted range sensing. Kerb transitions determine whether a route is usable by wheelchair users and people with reduced mobility, yet transitions are documented only sporadically. A vehicle-mounted range sensing platform surveyed 120 km of streets, and an extraction routine identified kerb transitions at every driveway, crossing and access point. Height, ramp presence and lateral gradient were computed for each transition and compared with regulatory limits. Manual verification at 250 transitions indicated agreement within two centimetres. Nearly a third of transitions were classified as non-compliant, and non-compliance was concentrated on routes serving older housing.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Segment-level noise exposure of pedestrians measured with body-worn dosimeters. Noise is consistently identified as a determinant of walking comfort but is rarely measured at the scale of the individual street segment. Participants carried calibrated personal noise dosimeters and GNSS loggers during their habitual walking trips over two weeks. Recordings were segmented by street and summarised as equivalent and percentile levels. Exposure varied by more than fifteen decibels between parallel routes of similar length, and participants systematically reported lower comfort on segments where measured levels exceeded a threshold identified from the data.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Estimating pedestrian shade provision using vehicle-mounted hemispherical imaging across seasons. Shade availability changes with foliage phenology, which single-date assessments cannot capture. Hemispherical images were captured at pedestrian height along fixed routes in leaf-on and leaf-off conditions using a vehicle-mounted rig. Canopy openness and projected shadow were computed for each condition and combined with solar geometry to estimate shade duration across the year. Seasonal variation was substantial on deciduous streets, and the resulting seasonal shade profiles were used to identify corridors where evergreen planting would extend usable shade.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Automated detection of pedestrian signal and crossing aids from street imagery in a medium-sized city. Provision of crossing aids is a determinant of route feasibility, particularly for older pedestrians and people with sensory impairment. Street imagery covering all signalised intersections was processed with a detection model trained to identify pedestrian signal heads, push buttons, audible signal devices and tactile indicators. Model output was verified at a random sample of sites. Audible devices were present at only 12 percent of signalised crossings, and provision was significantly lower outside the central district.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Detecting missing and damaged curb ramps from street-level imagery using an object detection network. Curb ramps are a prerequisite for barrier-free pedestrian travel, yet municipal inventories are frequently incomplete. This study fine-tuned a detection model on 14,000 annotated street-level images to locate curb ramps at intersections and to classify their condition as intact, damaged or absent. The model achieved a mean average precision of 0.81 on a held-out test set. Applied to an entire mid-sized city, the pipeline flagged 27 percent of intersections as lacking at least one compliant ramp, and results were verified by field inspection of a stratified sample.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Mapping sidewalk network continuity through semantic segmentation of street-level imagery. Pedestrian network datasets are absent or incomplete in most cities, which limits routing and equity analysis. We applied a semantic segmentation model to 210,000 street-level images to detect sidewalk presence on each side of every street segment, and reconstructed a topologically connected pedestrian network. Gaps were classified as physical discontinuity, occlusion, or genuine absence. The derived network revealed that 22 percent of residential streets lacked a continuous walking surface, with discontinuities clustering around arterial crossings and industrial land uses.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Deriving pedestrian route accessibility from terrestrial mobile mapping in a hilly city. Distance-based accessibility measures ignore vertical effort, which is decisive in topographically complex cities. A backpack mobile mapping system captured georeferenced point clouds along 45 km of pedestrian routes, from which continuous elevation profiles, step counts and handrail presence were extracted. An effort-weighted accessibility measure was then computed for routes connecting residential blocks to transit stops. Compared with planar distance, the effort-weighted measure reclassified 31 percent of connections as poorly accessible, particularly for older residents.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Detecting traffic exposure at pedestrian level using roadside sensing and image analysis. Pedestrian comfort and safety depend on proximity and speed of adjacent motor traffic. Roadside radar units recorded vehicle speeds and volumes at 42 street segments while street imagery was segmented to measure carriageway width, buffer presence and parking configuration. Combining the two data sources produced a segment-level traffic exposure indicator. Segments lacking any physical buffer showed exposure values three times higher than those with planted verges, and the indicator aligned with pedestrian counts observed at the same locations.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Mobile microclimate transects for mapping pedestrian thermal comfort at street level. Static weather stations poorly represent the thermal conditions experienced while walking. Instrumented carts and body-worn sensors recorded air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and globe temperature along repeated walking transects during summer afternoons. Universal Thermal Climate Index values were computed continuously and matched to street segments. Shaded segments with continuous tree canopy showed values up to 7 degrees lower than adjacent unshaded segments, and the resulting maps identified priority corridors for shading interventions.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Quantifying shade availability on sidewalks from mobile lidar and hemispherical imaging. Shade is a decisive determinant of walking comfort in hot climates, yet canopy cover measured from above does not indicate whether the walking surface itself is shaded. This work combined mobile lidar point clouds with hemispherical images captured at pedestrian height to reconstruct sky view factor and to simulate shadow projection onto the sidewalk across the day. Segment-level shade duration was validated against on-site pyranometer readings. Results showed that only 34 percent of the sidewalk network received more than four hours of shade during peak summer hours.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Personal exposure sensing of particulate matter along alternative pedestrian routes. Air quality shapes the healthfulness of walking but is usually inferred from sparse regulatory monitors. Volunteers carried calibrated low-cost particulate sensors and GNSS loggers along paired route alternatives between the same origins and destinations. Concentrations were aggregated by street segment and compared against traffic volume and street geometry. Routes through interior streets showed concentrations 28 percent lower than arterial alternatives of comparable length, demonstrating that route-level exposure differences are substantial and measurable.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Surface temperature of paving materials measured with pedestrian-height thermal imaging. Radiant heat from paving contributes to discomfort during summer walking but is not captured by air temperature alone. A tripod-mounted thermal camera recorded surface temperatures of different paving materials along footpaths at hourly intervals across clear summer days. Materials were classified from co-registered visible images. Dark impervious surfaces exceeded light permeable pavers by up to 15 degrees at midday, and the measured differentials were incorporated into a route-level heat exposure indicator.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Eye-level greenery and visual enclosure measured from panoramic street imagery. Overhead vegetation indices poorly represent the greenery actually visible to a pedestrian. This study processed 180,000 panoramic images with a segmentation network to compute green view index, sky view factor and building enclosure at eye level for every street segment in a dense district. Indicators were validated against on-site observer ratings at 150 locations. Eye-level greenery correlated only weakly with canopy cover derived from overhead sources, confirming that pedestrian-perspective measurement captures a distinct attribute of the walking environment.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Measuring active frontage and facade transparency at pedestrian scale using image segmentation. Ground-floor activity and visual permeability are recognised contributors to the pleasurability of walking. Street-level imagery was segmented to delineate ground-floor facade area, glazing, doorways and blank wall extent along 9,400 street segments. Indicators of frontage activity and transparency were computed and validated against manual audits. Segments with high transparency showed significantly higher observed pedestrian dwell activity recorded by fixed cameras, linking the measured attribute to observable use of the space.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Continuous monitoring of pedestrian thermal exposure using a network of fixed street-level sensors. Fixed monitoring at pedestrian height remains rare despite the importance of microclimate for walking comfort. Compact stations measuring air temperature, humidity, wind and globe temperature were mounted on light poles at pedestrian height at 32 locations for eighteen months. Universal Thermal Climate Index series were computed and compared with the reference airport station. Differences of up to six degrees were observed between instrumented streets under identical synoptic conditions, and the network captured the onset and duration of local heat episodes with far greater fidelity than the reference site.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Wearable physiological sensing to identify stressful segments of commuting walking routes. Physiological monitoring can localise where in a route discomfort arises. Commuters wore chest-mounted sensors capturing heart rate and electrodermal activity during habitual walking commutes over two weeks, with positions logged by satellite. Signals were normalised per participant and segment-level arousal indices were computed. Elevated arousal clustered at unsignalised crossings of arterial roads and at segments lacking a physical buffer from traffic, and clusters were reproducible across participants.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Ultraviolet exposure along pedestrian routes measured with wearable dosimeters. Ultraviolet exposure during daily walking has health implications yet is not represented in walkability assessment. Participants wore electronic ultraviolet dosimeters on the shoulder during habitual outdoor trips across a summer season, with position recorded concurrently. Segment-level exposure was computed and related to measured sky view factor and canopy cover. Routes with continuous canopy reduced cumulative exposure by more than half relative to open alternatives of equivalent duration.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension

text: Semantic segmentation for autonomous driving scene understanding with adaptive weighting. Accurate scene parsing is required for safe autonomous driving. This paper introduces a segmentation architecture with skip connections and an adaptive class weighting scheme to improve recognition of underrepresented classes including road, sidewalk and vegetation. Evaluation on standard driving benchmarks demonstrates improved mean intersection over union relative to baseline architectures while maintaining inference speed suitable for onboard deployment.
label: Not related

text: Pedestrian-level turbulence mapping beneath elevated transport structures. Fast-response anemometers were moved through a regular grid beneath viaducts and adjoining sidewalks under several prevailing wind directions. Peak turbulence intensity concentrated near column gaps and abrupt changes in deck height. These observations are important because elevated infrastructure can create uncomfortable wind jets and recirculation zones. The measurements reveal local conditions not represented by roof-level meteorological data.
label: Sensing of walkability dimension
